title: How to Read a Balance Sheet as an Investor
summary: How to read a balance sheet: what assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity mean, which lines to check first, and how to spot debt or cash pressure in a company's filing.
body_markdown:
There is no single good number. The SEC notes that desirable ratios vary by industry, so compare the company with its own earlier filings and with competitors' filings rather than with a rule of thumb.


The balance sheet also has limits. The SEC guide points out that an[income statement](https://meetbenson.com/blog/how-to-read-an-income-statement/) shows whether a company made a profit, a cash-flow statement shows whether it generated cash, and no one financial statement tells the complete story. A strong balance sheet says nothing by itself about whether the share price already assumes too much.
